42: "Why do I not write to you?"
And you call yourself learned, and ask a question like that.
You should have guessed that I am well — that is to say — in a word, I have made an acquaintance who has taken hold of my heart.
I have — I do not know.
43: To give you an orderly account of how I came to know the most lovable of women would be hard work.
I am a happy and contented man, and a poor historian.
44: Everyone describes his mistress that way.
And yet I cannot possibly tell you how perfect she is, or why she is so perfect.
Enough to say that she has captured every one of my senses.
45: So much simplicity with so much understanding — so gentle, and yet so firm — a mind so serene, and a life so full of activity.
46: But all this is ugly nonsense, and conveys not a single trait of her.
Another time — no, not another time; now, this very instant, I will tell you the whole of it.
Between ourselves, since I began this letter I have three times been on the point of throwing down my pen, ordering my horse, and riding out.
And yet I swore this morning that I would not ride today — and yet every moment I am running to the window to see how high the sun is.
47: I could not hold out. Go to her I must.
I am just back, Wilhelm; and while I take my supper I will write to you.
What a delight it was to my soul to see her among those dear, beautiful children — eight brothers and sisters!
48: But if I go on like this, you will be no wiser at the end of my letter than you were at the beginning.
Listen, then, and I will force myself to give you the details.
49: I told you the other day that I had got to know S—, the district judge, and that he had invited me to visit him in his retreat — or rather in his little kingdom.
But I put off going, and perhaps would never have gone, if chance had not shown me the treasure hidden away in that quiet place.
Some of our young people had got up a ball in the country, and I agreed to go.
I offered my arm for the evening to a pretty, agreeable, but rather ordinary girl from the neighbourhood.
It was settled that I should hire a carriage and call for Charlotte, with my partner and her aunt, to take them all to the ball.
As we drove through the park to the hunting-lodge, my companion told me I was about to meet a very charming young lady.
"Take care," the aunt added, "that you do not lose your heart."
"Because she is already engaged to a very worthy man," she answered, "who has gone to settle his affairs after his father's death, and will come into a considerable inheritance."
The information meant nothing to me.
When we reached the gate, the sun was setting behind the tops of the mountains.
The air was heavy, and the ladies said they feared a storm was coming, since masses of low black cloud were gathering on the horizon.
I calmed them by pretending to know the weather, though I had my own fears that our pleasure would be spoiled.
50: I got down, and a maid came to the door and asked us to wait a moment for her mistress.
I walked across the courtyard to a well-built house, went up the flight of steps in front, opened the door, and saw the most charming sight I have ever witnessed.
Six children, from eleven years old down to two, were running about the hall around a lady of middle height with a lovely figure, dressed in plain white with pink ribbons.
She was holding a rye loaf and cutting slices for the little ones around her, each according to age and appetite.
She did it gracefully and affectionately, and each of them waited for his turn with his hands out, shouting his thanks.
Some ran off at once to enjoy their supper; the gentler ones went out to the courtyard to see the strangers and look over the carriage their Charlotte was to drive away in.
"Pray forgive me for making you come for me, and for keeping the ladies waiting," she said.
"Dressing, and settling a few household matters before I go, made me forget my children's supper — and they will not take it from anyone but me."
I made some ordinary compliment, but my whole soul was taken up with her bearing, her voice, her manner.
I had hardly collected myself when she ran into her room to fetch her gloves and fan.
The children threw curious looks at me from a distance, and I went up to the youngest, a most delicious little creature.
He drew back; and Charlotte, coming in at that very moment, said, "Louis, shake hands with your cousin."
The little fellow did it willingly, and I could not resist giving him a hearty kiss, dirty face and all.
"Cousin," I said to Charlotte as I handed her down, "do you think I deserve the happiness of being related to you?"
She answered with a ready smile, "Oh! I have such a number of cousins that I should be sorry if you were the least deserving of them."
As she left, she told her next sister, Sophy, a girl of about eleven, to take good care of the children and to say goodbye to papa for her when he came home from his ride.
She told the little ones to obey their sister Sophy as they would obey her.
Some of them promised they would; but a little fair-haired girl of about six looked discontented and said, "But Sophy is not you, Charlotte; and we like you best."
The two eldest boys had climbed up onto the carriage, and at my asking she let them come with us a little way through the forest, on their promise to sit very still and hold on tight.
51: We were hardly seated, and the ladies had barely exchanged compliments about each other's dresses and about the company they expected to meet, when Charlotte stopped the carriage and made her brothers get down.
They insisted on kissing her hands once more — the elder with all the tenderness of a boy of fifteen, the other more lightly and carelessly.
She sent her love to the children again, and we drove off.
52: The aunt asked Charlotte whether she had finished the book she had sent her last.
"No," said Charlotte. "I did not like it; you can have it back."
"And the one before it was not much better."
I was surprised, when I asked the title, to hear that it was ____.
(We feel obliged to suppress this passage in the letter, so that no one should feel aggrieved — though no author need pay much heed to the opinion of a mere girl, or of an unsteady young man.)
53: I found insight and character in everything she said.
Every turn of phrase seemed to light up her face with fresh charm, with fresh rays of genius, unfolding by degrees as she felt herself understood.
54: "When I was younger," she said, "I loved nothing so much as novels."
"Nothing could equal my delight when, on some holiday, I could settle quietly into a corner and enter with my whole heart and soul into the joys and sorrows of some imaginary Leonora."
"I will not deny that they still have some charm for me."
"But I read so seldom now that I prefer books exactly suited to my taste."

"And I like those authors best whose scenes describe my own situation in life, and the people around me — whose stories interest me because they resemble my own homely existence, which, without being paradise, is on the whole a source of indescribable happiness."
55: I tried to hide the emotion these words stirred in me, but with little success.
When she had spoken so truly about "The Vicar of Wakefield," and about other works whose names I leave out, I could contain myself no longer and gave full utterance to what I thought of them.
(Though the names are omitted, the authors mentioned deserve Charlotte's approval, and will feel it in their hearts when they read this passage.
It was not until Charlotte turned to the other two ladies that I remembered they were there, and saw them sitting mute with astonishment.
The aunt looked at me several times with an air of mockery, which I did not mind in the least.
56: We talked about the pleasures of dancing.
"If it is a fault to love it," said Charlotte, "then I confess I value it above every other amusement."
"If anything troubles me, I go to the piano and play an air I have danced to, and everything comes right again at once."
57: You, who know me, can imagine how steadily I looked into her rich dark eyes while she said all this.

You can imagine how my whole soul feasted on her warm lips and fresh, glowing cheeks, and how completely I was lost in the lovely meaning of her words — so lost that I hardly heard the words themselves.
In short, I got out of the carriage like a man in a dream, and was so far gone from the dim world around me that I hardly heard the music coming down from the lighted ballroom.
58: The two Messrs. Andran, and a certain N. N. — I cannot trouble myself with the names — were the aunt's and Charlotte's partners.
They met us at the carriage door and took charge of their ladies, while I followed with mine.
59: I led out one lady after another, and precisely the most disagreeable of them could not bring themselves to stop.
Charlotte and her partner began an English country dance, and you can imagine my delight when their turn came to dance the figure with us.
She dances with her whole heart and soul.
Her whole figure is harmony, elegance, and grace, as though she were conscious of nothing else and had no other thought or feeling — and no doubt, for that moment, every other sensation is put out.
60: She was engaged for the second country dance, but promised me the third, and told me with the most agreeable frankness that she loved to waltz.
"It is the custom here," she said, "for the previous partners to waltz together; but my partner waltzes badly, and will be delighted if I spare him the trouble."
"Your partner is not allowed to waltz, and cannot do it either; but I noticed during the country dance that you waltz well."
"So if you will waltz with me, do propose it to my partner, and I will propose it to yours."
We agreed, and it was settled that our partners should entertain each other.
61: We set off, and at first delighted ourselves with the usual graceful movements of the arms.
With what grace, with what ease she moved!
When the waltz itself began, and the dancers whirled around each other in the giddy maze, there was some confusion, because several of them could not manage it.
We were wise and held back, letting the others tire themselves out.
When the clumsy ones had withdrawn, we joined in and kept it up splendidly, together with one other couple — Andran and his partner.
Never have I danced more lightly.
I felt more than mortal, holding the loveliest of creatures in my arms, flying with her as fast as the wind until everything else was lost to sight.
And oh, Wilhelm, I swore at that moment that a girl I loved, or felt the slightest attachment to, should never waltz with anyone but me, if I were damned for it.
62: We took a few turns about the room to get our breath back.
Charlotte sat down and refreshed herself with some oranges I had managed to secure — the only ones left.
But at every slice she politely offered to her neighbours, I felt as though a dagger went through my heart.
63: We were the second couple in the third country dance.

As we were going down the line — and Heaven knows with what ecstasy I looked at her arms and her eyes, shining with the sweetest feeling of pure and genuine enjoyment — we passed a lady whose charming expression I had noticed, though she was no longer young.
She looked at Charlotte with a smile, held up a finger in a threatening way, and said the name "Albert" twice, in a very meaningful tone.
64: "Who is Albert," I said to Charlotte, "if it is not impertinent to ask?"
She was about to answer when we had to separate for a figure of the dance; and as we crossed in front of each other again, I thought she looked thoughtful.
"Why should I hide it from you?" she said, giving me her hand for the promenade.
"Albert is a worthy man, and I am engaged to him."
There was nothing new to me in this — the girls had told me on the way.
But it was new in this sense: I had not thought of it in connection with her, whom I had come in so short a time to value so highly.

Enough; I became confused, lost my place in the figure, and threw everyone into disorder, so that it took all Charlotte's presence of mind to set me right by pulling and pushing me back where I belonged.
65: The dance was not yet over when the lightning, which had been showing on the horizon for some time and which I had insisted was nothing but heat, grew fiercer, and the thunder drowned the music.

When fear or distress overtakes us in the middle of our amusements, it naturally makes a deeper impression than at other times — either because the contrast makes us more sensitive, or, more likely, because our senses are then wide open and the shock strikes harder.
To that I must put down the fright and the shrieking of the ladies.
One sat down shrewdly in a corner with her back to the window and stopped her ears with her fingers.
A second knelt in front of her and hid her face in her lap; a third pushed in between them and embraced her sister in floods of tears.

Some insisted on going home; others hardly knew what they were doing, and had too little presence of mind to check the impertinence of their young partners, who were busy turning onto themselves the sighs their agitated beauties meant for heaven.
Some of the gentlemen had gone downstairs for a quiet cigar, and the rest of the company gladly took up the hostess's happy suggestion of moving into another room that had shutters and curtains.
We had hardly got there when Charlotte set the chairs in a circle; and when the company had sat down at her request, she proposed a round game.
66: I noticed some of the company purse their mouths and draw themselves up at the prospect of an agreeable forfeit.
"Let us play at counting," said Charlotte.
"Now pay attention. I shall go round the circle from right to left, and each person is to count, one after another, the number that falls to him — and you must count fast."
"Whoever stops or makes a mistake gets a box on the ear, and so on, until we have counted to a thousand."
It was delightful to watch.
She went round the circle with her arm raised.
"One," said the first; "two," the second; "three," the third; and so on, while Charlotte went faster and faster.
Someone made a mistake, and instantly a box on the ear; and in the laughter that followed, another box; and so on, faster and faster.
I came in for two myself.
I fancied they were harder than the rest, and was quite delighted.
General laughter and confusion broke up the game long before we had counted as far as a thousand.
The party split into little separate knots.
The storm had passed, and I followed Charlotte into the ballroom.
On the way she said, "The game drove away their fear of the storm."
I could make no reply.
"I was as frightened as any of them," she went on, "but by putting on courage to keep the others up, I forgot my own fears."
We went to the window.
It was still thundering in the distance.
A soft rain was falling over the country and filling the air around us with delicious scents.
Charlotte leaned forward on her arm, her eyes wandering over the scene.
She raised them to the sky, then turned them on me; they were wet with tears.
She put her hand on mine and said, "Klopstock!"
At once I remembered the magnificent ode that was in her mind, and I sank under the weight of everything I felt.
It was more than I could bear.
I bent over her hand, kissed it in a stream of delicious tears, and looked up into her eyes again.
Divine Klopstock! Why did you not see your apotheosis in those eyes?
And your name, so often profaned — would that I might never hear it spoken again!
